entry.title: What the Guest Wants
entry.summary: By the seventh day the province had a name for it. They called it the quiet sickness, because it did not announce itself. There was no wasting, no lesions, no dramatic collapse. A man would feel a heaviness, then a pressure, and then — according to the physicians, who had begun to write reports in the flat language of people who had run out of explanations — a change in manner. The reports used the word carefully. Not madness. Not possession. Manner. One of the affected was a clerk in the eastern administration...

entry.title: The Quiet Sickness
entry.summary: Ajax did not tell the physician about the second sensation. He had come close. The man had asked whether anything unusual had happened, and Ajax had opened his mouth to describe a pressure that did not belong to him, a presence that had answered once in the dark and then gone quiet. Then he had looked at the physician's face — tired, harried, already carrying forty other patients — and said instead that he was tired. entry.summary: The invitation arrived three days after the Wilhelmshire family had resumed having breakfast together. It was delivered in a dark blue envelope, bearing the royal crest in silver. Ajax noticed it before anyone else. "That looks expensive." His father, who had been reading the accompanying letter, glanced at him. "It is an invitation." "I gathered that much from the envelope." entry.title: A Faint Trace
entry.summary: Ten days had passed since Ajax first began noticing traces of energy without the assistance of a crystal. Ten days of experiments, observations, and considerably more patience than he had initially expected to require. His progress, however, remained difficult to measure. He could recognise the sensation now. Not consistently, and certainly not whenever he wished, but he had begun to distinguish it from the ordinary impressions produced by his surroundings. entry.title: Learning to Feel
entry.summary: The garden was quiet in the early morning. Ajax sat beneath the shade of an orchid tree, his wheelchair positioned beside a small stone table. Beyond the garden, the road in front of the Wilhelmshire estate stretched towards the distant city. Rows of orchid trees stood along the outer wall, their branches covered in clusters of pink blossoms. A few petals drifted through the air. Cars passed along the road at regular intervals.
